planting.note: Direct sow in early spring as soon as soil can be worked, surface-sowing lightly since seed needs light and cool soil to germinate; self-sows readily once established.

directions: Sow directly into fertile, nitrogen-rich, moisture-retentive soil in full sun to partial shade; unlike the perennial, rhizome-spreading stinging nettle, dwarf nettle is a true annual that completes its lifecycle from seed each year and dies after setting seed. Its sting is often reported as sharper and more immediately painful than that of common stinging nettle, so wear gloves and long sleeves when handling or harvesting. Historically used in European folk medicine and homeopathy (as the source of the remedy Urtica urens) and sometimes grown for compost-tea and liquid-feed production, though it is less favored than Urtica dioica for culinary use. Allow a few plants to self-seed if naturalizing in an out-of-the-way bed, or deadhead before seed-set to prevent spread.

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped stock in early spring or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; tolerates heavier shade than most hornbeams once established.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in full sun to light shade, sheltering from drying winds while young. Native to the mountain forests of Japan, Korea, and northeastern China, heartleaf hornbeam is distinguished from its relatives by unusually large, deeply pleated, heart-shaped leaves up to 5 inches long and by its showy, hop-like fruiting clusters (strobiles) that hang in dense, pendulous chains through summer and fall. Fall color develops into rich yellow tones. It grows slowly into a broad, rounded small tree and is prized by collectors as a specimen or understory planting in woodland and Asian-themed gardens. Avoid heavy, poorly drained clay, which stresses the shallow root system.

planting.note: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline, rocky or loamy, lean to average soil in full sun; give excellent drainage since this species is adapted to thin mountain limestone soils.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average, slightly alkaline soil in full sun, where this slow-growing conifer can develop its dense, compact, pyramidal to rounded crown of short, stiff, blue-green needles. Cedrus brevifolia is endemic to the Tripylos and Paphos Forest region of the Troodos Mountains on Cyprus, where it survives today only in restricted native stands; it is treated by many botanists as a geographically isolated subspecies or close relative of Cedar of Lebanon but is distinguished horticulturally by its notably shorter needles, smaller cones, and more compact, slower-growing habit, making it well suited to smaller gardens than the larger true cedars. Tolerates heat, drought, and alkaline soils once established; avoid wet, poorly drained sites.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew — Conifer Database

planting.note: Direct sow or plant transplants after soil has warmed following the last frost in moist to wet, fertile soil in full sun; pods should be removed promptly where naturalization is a concern, as this species seeds aggressively along waterways in warm climates.

directions: Plant in moist to wet, fertile soil in full sun along pond margins, ditch banks, or other consistently damp sites where this fast-growing, short-lived shrub can show off its drooping clusters of brick-red to orange, wisteria-like pea flowers in late spring and summer. Native to South America, red sesbania has naturalized widely in the warm, wet lowlands of the southeastern United States and South Africa, where it is now regulated as invasive in some jurisdictions, so site it only where seed spread along waterways can be monitored and controlled. The flowers are followed by distinctive four-winged, papery seed pods that persist and rattle in the wind, giving rise to the common name rattlebox. All plant parts, especially the seeds, are toxic if ingested.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun; give it room for its graceful, broad pyramidal crown of long, pendulous, drooping branchlets to develop unobstructed.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun, where this graceful conifer, native to central and southern China, can develop its characteristic weeping habit of long, drooping, cord-like branchlets clothed in flattened, soft, bright green scale-like foliage. Long cultivated in Chinese temple gardens and cemeteries — hence the common name mourning or funeral cypress — it is among the most ornamentally refined and weeping of all true cypresses, lending a graceful, cascading texture distinct from the stiffly upright habit of Italian cypress. Establishes best with regular watering through its first two summers, after which it tolerates heat and moderate drought; avoid heavy, waterlogged soils, which quickly lead to root rot.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew — Conifer Database

planting.note: Plant container-grown offsets or nursery stock in spring in well-drained, sandy, average to lean soil in full sun to partial shade; extremely slow to establish from seed, so most gardeners start from nursery-grown plants.

directions: Plant in well-drained, sandy, lean to average soil in full sun to dappled shade, mimicking the understory conditions of the southwestern Australian jarrah and karri forests where this cycad grows naturally beneath eucalypts. Macrozamia riedlei forms a stout, mostly underground trunk topped by a dense rosette of stiff, dark green, pinnate fronds, eventually producing large barrel-shaped cones at the crown center on mature plants, with male and female plants bearing distinctly different cone types. Extremely slow-growing and long-lived, it is highly drought-tolerant once established and rarely needs supplemental feeding, making it a durable architectural accent for dry, low-maintenance landscape plantings in mild-winter climates. All parts, especially the seeds, are toxic if ingested by people or animals.
sources: Kings Park and Botanic Garden, Western Australia
Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew — Cycad Pages
